title: Confucius and Laozi in Dialogue
bigQuestion: Where do the Confucian and Daoist classics truly disagree, where do they overlap, and how have Chinese readers held them together?

story.title: Two Quotations on a Board
story.kicker: Two sayings about repaying injury go up side by side, and the class splits.
paragraphs: Ms. Lin writes two short sayings on the whiteboard of her twelfth-grade philosophy class in suburban Chicago. She does not say where they come from. The first: someone asks whether injury should be repaid with kindness, and the answer is, repay injury with justice, and kindness with kindness. The second: repay injury with kindness.

She asks the class to stand on the side of the room that matches the saying they find more convincing. About half the students walk to the window side, under the first saying. The rest go to the door side, under the second. A few stand in the middle and refuse to choose.

Then she reveals the sources. The first is Analects 14.36, a saying of Confucius. The second is from chapter 63 of the Daodejing. Several students are surprised. One says he thought the Daodejing was the book about fairness. Another says she assumed Confucius would be the gentle one.

Ms. Lin tells them the two lines have been read together for centuries. Some commentators think the Analects passage answers the Daodejing's line directly. Others doubt that and say the ideas were simply in the air. She asks each side to explain what the other side's saying gets right. The room gets quieter as they think.
story.think: What does "repay injury with justice" protect that "repay injury with kindness" might risk? What does the second protect that the first might risk?

lessons.title: Two Starting Points
lessons.mainIdea: The Analects often starts from ritual and learning that shape a person, while the Daodejing often starts from naturalness that learning and ritual can spoil.
reading: Analects 12.1 says ren is to subdue oneself and return to propriety, li. Analects 1.1 opens with the pleasure of constant learning. The Confucian picture often starts from shaping: people become good through study, ritual and good models. A person is carved and polished over time.

The Daodejing often starts elsewhere. Chapter 19 urges people to cast off "sageliness" and cleverness so the people benefit. Chapter 38 calls ritual the thin edge of loyalty and the start of disorder. Chapter 28 praises returning to the "uncarved block," *pu*, raw wood not yet shaped. Its picture often values what is natural before shaping.

These are tendencies, not walls. The Analects also warns that ritual without feeling is empty (3.3). The Daodejing also speaks of the sage's care and "three treasures." Scholars warn against turning the books into cartoons of rule-follower and free spirit. The disagreement is real, but both books share concern for a good and peaceful life.

words.d: "the uncarved block"; raw wood, a Daodejing image of simplicity before shaping
ritual and proper conduct; Legge's "propriety"
ziran; being so of oneself, without forced shaping
a usual direction or leaning, not an absolute rule

look.title: Carved or Uncarved?
look.text: Analects 1.15 (paraphrased): a disciple quotes a poem about cutting, filing, carving and polishing jade, and the Master praises him for seeing it as a picture of self-cultivation. Daodejing 28 (paraphrased): return to the uncarved block.
look.prompt: What does each image value? Could a person hold both at once? How?

check.q: What does pu, the uncarved block, stand for in the Daodejing?
check.why: Pu is raw wood, an image of natural simplicity.

check.q: What does Daodejing 38 say about ritual?
choices: It is the root of all goodness
It is the thin edge of loyalty and the start of disorder
It is the same as the Dao
check.why: Chapter 38 is wary of ritual.

check.q: Why does the lesson call these "tendencies, not walls"?
choices: Both books were written by the same person
Each book has passages that soften the contrast
check.why: The Analects also warns against empty ritual; the Daodejing also speaks of care.

lessons.title: When Confucius Met Laozi
lessons.mainIdea: Sima Qian's Records of the Historian tells of Confucius visiting Laozi to ask about ritual, a meeting scholars treat as legend but which shaped how the two were seen.
reading: The historian Sima Qian, writing around 100 BCE in the Shiji, the Records of the Historian, tells a story in chapter 63. Confucius travels to the Zhou capital to ask Laozi about ritual. Laozi tells him to set aside his proud airs and many desires. Afterward Confucius tells his disciples that Laozi is like a dragon, beyond his understanding.

Most modern scholars treat the meeting as a *legend*: a traditional story that may not be historical. Sima Qian himself admitted uncertainty about Laozi's identity. Still, other early texts, including Confucian ritual records, also mention Confucius learning from a Lao Dan about rites. The story may preserve some old tradition.

The legend shaped how Chinese readers saw the two teachers: an elder sage and a younger one, not enemies. Artists in the Han dynasty carved the meeting on tomb stones. Religious Daoists told it with honor for Laozi. Confucian readers told it with honor for Confucius's humility in asking. Each told it their own way.

words.d: Records of the Historian, Sima Qian's history of China, completed c. 90s BCE
a traditional story that may or may not be historically true
the Han dynasty historian (c. 145–c. 86 BCE) who wrote the Shiji

look.title: Like a Dragon
look.text: After meeting Laozi, Confucius told his disciples that he knew how birds fly, fish swim and beasts run, and how each can be caught; but a dragon rides the wind and clouds up to heaven, and he could not know it. Laozi, he said, was like a dragon.
look.cite: Sima Qian, Shiji ch. 63 (Biography of Laozi), c. 90s BCE; paraphrased for this course
look.prompt: How does this story honor Laozi? How might a Confucian reader still find honor for Confucius in it?

check.q: What did Confucius ask Laozi about, in Sima Qian's story?
check.why: Confucius went to ask about rites.

check.q: How do most modern scholars treat the meeting?
choices: As a legend that may not be historical
check.why: Scholars treat it as legend, though it may keep an old tradition.

check.q: What did Confucius compare Laozi to?
check.why: In the Shiji, Confucius says Laozi is like a dragon.

lessons.title: Confucius in the Zhuangzi
lessons.mainIdea: The Zhuangzi uses Confucius as a character, sometimes teasing him and sometimes making him voice Daoist ideas.
reading: Confucius appears many times in the Zhuangzi as a character. In some stories he is corrected by hermits, fishermen or robbers. In chapter 29, the robber Zhi sends him away with a scolding. These stories poke fun at Confucian concern for rank, office and ritual.

In other stories Confucius becomes a Daoist teacher. In chapter 4 he teaches Yan Hui the "fasting of the mind," emptying oneself to meet the world. In chapter 6, Yan Hui tells Confucius he has learned "sitting and forgetting." Confucius is so impressed that he asks to become Yan Hui's follower.

Readers explain this in different ways. Some see mockery. Some see respect: the Zhuangzi borrows Confucius's authority to teach its own ideas. Some later scholars, including Guo Xiang, argued that the Zhuangzi secretly honored Confucius as the true sage. The book's playful use of a real teacher is itself a kind of *dialogue* between schools.

words.d: a Zhuangzi ch. 4 practice of emptying the mind, taught by Confucius as a character
zuowang; a Zhuangzi ch. 6 practice of letting go of the self, described by Yan Hui
a conversation, here between schools of thought
humor used to point out faults

look.title: Confucius as a Character
look.text: Zhuangzi 6 (paraphrased): Yan Hui says he has forgotten ritual and music; Confucius says good, but not yet. Later Yan Hui says he can "sit and forget." Confucius, amazed, asks to follow him.
look.prompt: Is this story mocking Confucius, honoring him, or using him? Point to details that support your reading.

check.q: What does Confucius teach in Zhuangzi chapter 4?
check.why: In chapter 4 Confucius teaches Yan Hui the fasting of the mind.

check.q: In Zhuangzi chapter 6, what does Confucius ask after Yan Hui describes sitting and forgetting?
check.why: Confucius, impressed, asks to follow Yan Hui.

check.q: What did Guo Xiang argue about the Zhuangzi and Confucius?
choices: The book secretly honored Confucius as the true sage
check.why: Guo Xiang read the Zhuangzi as honoring Confucius at a deeper level.

lessons.title: Justice for Injury
lessons.mainIdea: In Analects 14.36, the Master rejects repaying injury with kindness and says to repay injury with justice and kindness with kindness.
reading: Analects 14.36 is a short exchange. Legge: "Some one said, 'What do you say concerning the principle that injury should be recompensed with kindness?' The Master said, 'With what then will you recompense kindness? Recompense injury with justice, and recompense kindness with kindness.'"

The Master's answer turns on a question of balance. If injury gets kindness, what is left for kindness? Legge's "justice" translates zhi, which also means straightness or uprightness. Some translators write "uprightness" or "straightness." The idea is to respond to injury honestly and fairly, not with revenge and not with a show of favor.

Readers note that the questioner may be quoting a known saying. Some commentators link it to Daodejing 63. Others say the idea was common and cannot be traced to one book. Either way, 14.36 shows the Analects valuing *proportion*: a response that fits what was done.

words.d: uprightness or straightness; Legge's "justice" in Analects 14.36
to repay or give back in return
a fitting balance between an act and the response to it

look.title: With What Will You Recompense Kindness?
look.text: Some one said, 'What do you say concerning the principle that injury should be recompensed with kindness?' The Master said, 'With what then will you recompense kindness? Recompense injury with justice, and recompense kindness with kindness.'
look.cite: Confucian Analects 14.36, trans. James Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 1, 2nd ed., 1893
look.prompt: What problem does the Master see in repaying injury with kindness? What does "justice" mean here, and what does it not mean?

check.q: What does the Master say to recompense injury with in 14.36?
check.why: Legge: "Recompense injury with justice."

check.q: What Chinese word does Legge translate "justice" in 14.36?
check.why: Zhi means straightness or uprightness.

check.q: What value does 14.36 show, according to the lesson?
choices: Proportion: a response that fits what was done
check.why: The Master keeps kindness for kindness and uprightness for injury.

lessons.title: Kindness for Injury
lessons.mainIdea: Daodejing chapter 63 includes repaying injury with kindness among the sage's ways of acting without forcing.
reading: Chapter 63 is a list of paradoxes. Act without acting. Handle affairs without fuss. Taste the tasteless. Treat the small as great and the few as many. And, in the same list, repay injury with kindness, or with *de*, virtue. The line sits among ways the sage handles things before they grow large.

The chapter goes on to say that hard things should be handled while they are easy, and great things while they are small. Read in context, repaying injury with kindness may be part of this: meeting harm early and gently so it does not grow. Some readers take it as a moral ideal. Others take it as practical wisdom.

Many readers have compared this line with the Christian teaching to love one's enemies (Matthew 5:44) and with Buddhist teachings on returning hatred with non-hatred. Scholars caution that similar words can have different reasons behind them. Comparing them well means asking why each tradition says it.

words.d: virtue or power; in ch. 63, the kindness with which the sage repays injury
read together with the words around it
a picture of what is best, which people aim toward

look.title: Chapter 63
look.text: Act without striving; handle affairs without fuss; taste what has no flavor. Treat the small as great and the few as many. Repay injury with kindness. Deal with the hard while it is easy, and with the great while it is small.
look.cite: Daodejing ch. 63, paraphrased for this course; compare Legge, The Tao Teh King, Sacred Books of the East vol. 39, 1891
look.prompt: Does reading the line inside this list change what "repay injury with kindness" means? How?

check.q: What does Daodejing 63 say to repay injury with?
check.why: Chapter 63 lists repaying injury with kindness.

check.q: What kind of list surrounds the line in chapter 63?
choices: A list of paradoxes about acting without forcing
check.why: Chapter 63 lists paradoxes like acting without acting.

check.q: What does the lesson warn about comparing ch. 63 with other traditions?
choices: They are exactly the same teaching
Similar words can have different reasons behind them
check.why: Good comparison asks why each tradition says what it says.

lessons.title: Weighing the Two Lines
lessons.mainIdea: Readers have long set Analects 14.36 beside Daodejing 63, and they disagree about whether one answers the other.
reading: Put the two lines side by side. The Analects keeps separate responses for injury and kindness. The Daodejing gives kindness to both. On the surface they contradict. Many readers treat this pair as a clean example of a Confucian and a Daoist difference.

Commentators have gone further. Some said the questioner in 14.36 was quoting Laozi, so Confucius was answering him. Others noted that we cannot date the two texts precisely, so we cannot say who answered whom. Scholars today usually say the idea of repaying injury with kindness was known in the period and appears in both.

Readers also ask whether the lines are about the same situation. The Analects may address public justice and relationships among equals. The Daodejing may address a sage's way of stopping conflict early. Reading each in its *context* can soften the contradiction without erasing it. The class in the story was right to find both lines hard.

words.d: two statements that cannot both be true in the same way
the words and setting around a passage that shape its meaning
working out when a text was written

look.title: Same Situation?
look.text: Case 1: a classmate spreads a false rumor about you. Case 2: two neighboring villages quarrel over water. Analects 14.36: repay injury with uprightness. Daodejing 63: repay injury with kindness, while problems are small.
look.prompt: Apply each line to each case. Does either line fit one case better than the other?

check.q: Why can scholars not say for sure who answered whom?
choices: The two texts cannot be dated precisely
check.why: Uncertain dating makes the order unclear.

check.q: How can reading in context soften the contradiction?
choices: The lines may address different situations
It shows the lines are the same
check.why: Public justice and a sage's early care for conflict may be different cases.

check.q: What do scholars today usually say about the idea of repaying injury with kindness?
choices: It was known in the period and appears in both texts
It is only in the Analects
check.why: The idea seems to have circulated widely.

sections.title: Rule, Religion and the Three Teachings

lessons.title: Virtue or Non-Interference?
lessons.mainIdea: The Analects pictures a ruler who leads by visible virtue; the Daodejing pictures one who governs by not interfering.
reading: Analects 2.1 makes the ruler a pole star all others turn toward. Analects 12.19 says the junzi's virtue is like wind and the people's like grass: the grass bends when the wind blows. In both images the ruler is seen and followed. Leadership is a matter of *example*.

Daodejing 17 prefers a ruler the people hardly know. Chapter 57 says the sage does not act and the people change by themselves. Chapter 60 warns against stirring the small fish. In these images the ruler steps back. Leadership is a matter of restraint.

Readers find common ground. Both books reject rule by force and fear. Both put the ruler's own character first. Both, in different ways, trust that good order grows rather than being imposed. The difference is how visible the ruler should be. Later Chinese statesmen often drew on both.

words.d: a model others copy; in the Analects, the ruler's visible virtue
holding back from acting or interfering
non-action or acting without forcing

look.title: Wind and Grass
look.text: The relation between superiors and inferiors, is like that between the wind and the grass. The grass must bend, when the wind blows across it.
look.cite: Confucian Analects 12.19, trans. James Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 1, 2nd ed., 1893
look.prompt: Compare this image with Daodejing 17's ruler whom the people barely know. Which ruler is more visible? Which relies more on example?

check.q: In Analects 12.19, what is the relation between superiors and inferiors compared to?
check.why: Legge's 12.19 uses wind and grass.

check.q: Where do both books agree about ruling?
choices: Both reject rule by force and fear
check.why: Both put character above force.

check.q: How does the Daodejing's ideal ruler differ from the Analects'?
choices: He steps back and is hardly known
check.why: Daodejing 17 praises the ruler the people barely know.

lessons.title: Is Confucianism a Religion?
lessons.mainIdea: Scholars and practitioners disagree about whether Confucianism is a religion, and the answer depends partly on what "religion" means.
reading: Consider the evidence people point to. Confucian temples stand in many cities, and ceremonies honor Confucius each year. Families offer rites to ancestors. The Analects speaks of Heaven, Tian. Yet the Analects also says the Master did not talk about spirits (7.20) and urges respect for spirits while keeping them at a distance (6.20).

Views differ. Legge, in The Religions of China (1880), treated Confucianism as a religion. The sociologist C. K. Yang described Chinese religion as "diffused": spread through family and state rather than gathered in one church. The reformer Kang Youwei, in the 1910s, tried to make Confucianism China's state religion. Many scholars call it a philosophy or a way of life.

Practitioners disagree too. Some see their rites as religious devotion. Others see them as family memory and ethics. The question also depends on the word *religion*, which grew up in Europe with Christianity in mind. This course names these views and does not settle the question.

words.d: a word with contested definitions; often beliefs and practices about the sacred
C. K. Yang's term for religion spread through family and state life rather than a separate church
a reformer (1858–1927) who tried to make Confucianism China's state religion

look.title: Sort the Evidence
look.text: A temple ceremony on Confucius's birthday. Analects 7.20: the Master did not talk about spirits. A family offering incense at an ancestor tablet. Analects 6.20: respect spirits but keep them at a distance. A philosophy course at a university.
look.prompt: Sort these into evidence a "religion" view would use and evidence a "philosophy" view would use. Which items could fit both?

check.q: What did C. K. Yang mean by "diffused religion"?
choices: Religion spread through family and state life
check.why: Yang described religion woven into social institutions.

check.q: Who tried to make Confucianism China's state religion in the 1910s?
check.why: Kang Youwei led that effort.

check.q: Why does the lesson say the word "religion" matters to the debate?
choices: It grew up in Europe with Christianity in mind
check.why: The category itself shapes the answer.

lessons.title: The Three Teachings as One
lessons.mainIdea: Many Chinese people have practiced Confucian, Daoist and Buddhist teachings together, a view summed up in the phrase "the three teachings are one."
reading: In many Chinese towns, one family might honor ancestors with Confucian rites, visit a Daoist temple for a festival, and invite Buddhist monks to chant at a funeral. Some temples hold images of Confucius, Laozi and the Buddha side by side. The phrase *sanjiao heyi*, "the three teachings are one," names this outlook.

Thinkers argued for it in different ways. Some said each teaching covered a different area: Confucianism for society, Daoism for the body, Buddhism for the mind. In the Ming dynasty, Lin Zhao'en founded a "Three-in-One" teaching that still has temples in Fujian and Southeast Asia. Others kept the teachings separate and argued for one over the others.

This outlook challenges the habit of treating religions as exclusive boxes. Scholars use terms like *syncretism*, the blending of traditions, but some think the word is too simple for Chinese practice. For many families, the question "which one are you?" does not fit how they live.

words.d: Confucianism, Daoism and Buddhism
"the three teachings are one"; the view that the three work together
the blending of different religious or philosophical traditions
a Ming dynasty teacher (1517–1598) who founded the Three-in-One teaching

look.title: One Family, Three Teachings
look.text: At Lunar New Year, a family in Chicago's Chinatown bows before ancestor tablets at home, visits a temple where incense is offered, and later attends a Buddhist memorial service for a grandparent.
look.prompt: Which of the three teachings might each practice connect to? Why might the family resist choosing just one label?

check.q: What does sanjiao heyi mean?
check.why: Sanjiao heyi names the unity of the three teachings.

check.q: Who founded the Three-in-One teaching in the Ming dynasty?
check.why: Lin Zhao'en founded it; it still has temples today.

check.q: Why do some scholars find the word "syncretism" too simple?
choices: It may not capture how Chinese practice actually works
check.why: Some think the term treats living practice as a mixture of separate boxes.

lessons.title: Comparing Without Ranking
lessons.mainIdea: A good comparison of the two classics describes differences and overlaps accurately and lets each speak in its own terms.
reading: Comparison can go wrong in two ways. One is flattening: saying the two books are really the same. The other is cartooning: making one book all rules and the other all freedom. Both miss what the texts say. A careful comparison names real differences and real overlaps.

A simple method helps. Pick one question, such as how to respond to injury or how to rule. Find a passage in each book. Quote or paraphrase each exactly. Describe what each says in its own terms. Then name one difference and one overlap, and describe how readers in each tradition have handled them.

What you should not do is declare a winner. This is not because the question is unimportant. It is because a public school course studies what traditions teach, not which is true. Your job is to make each position as clear and strong as its best readers would. Philosophers call this the principle of *charity*.

words.d: wrongly treating different ideas as if they were the same
making a view look simpler or sillier than it is
in reading, presenting a view in its strongest, fairest form

look.title: Build a Fair Comparison
look.text: Question: how should one respond to injury? Analects 14.36: repay injury with uprightness, kindness with kindness. Daodejing 63: repay injury with kindness. One difference: ______. One overlap: ______.
look.prompt: Fill in the blanks. Then write one sentence each side's best reader might say about the other.

check.q: What is "flattening" in comparison?
choices: Treating different ideas as the same
check.why: Flattening erases real differences.

check.q: What is the principle of charity in reading?
choices: Presenting a view in its strongest, fairest form
Choosing the kindest view as true
check.why: Charity means making each position as clear and strong as possible.

check.q: Why does this course not declare a winner between the traditions?
choices: It studies what traditions teach, not which is true
check.why: Public school study describes; it does not rule on truth.

review.q: Which passage says to recompense injury with justice?
Which passage includes repaying injury with kindness?
review.why: Chapter 63 lists it among the sage's ways.

review.q: Who told the story of Confucius visiting Laozi?
What does pu, the uncarved block, stand for?
review.why: Pu is a Daodejing image of natural simplicity.

review.q: In which book does Confucius teach the fasting of the mind?
review.why: Zhuangzi ch. 4 makes Confucius teach it.

review.q: What image does Analects 12.19 use for a leader's influence?
review.why: Legge: the grass must bend when the wind blows.

review.q: Which scholar described Chinese religion as "diffused"?
review.why: C. K. Yang used the term.

review.q: What does "the three teachings are one" refer to?
review.why: Sanjiao heyi unites the three teachings.
